text: Lecture twenty: Controlled inputs. Letting state decide what every box shows. The interview question behind this lecture is a core one, and you will hear it a lot. How do you make an input, a text area, or a select fully controlled by React state? First, the overview. Why a form needs its text in state. And we begin small: a name, a greeting, and a Clear button. Here is a tiny page with one box, one greeting, and one button. When the page opens, the box is empty. In figure one, the browser shows localhost:5173. There's a label, Name, with an empty box next to it. Under that, a line that just says, "Hello," with a comma and nothing after it, and then a Clear button. This is all the code behind it in App.jsx, and it's short. Line one imports useState from React. Line three starts our component, App. Line four makes a piece of state called name with its setter, setName, and it starts as an empty string. Then the page itself. Inside a main tag, there's a label with the word Name, and inside the label on line ten, the input. It gets value equals name in curly braces and an onChange that takes the event e and calls setName with e.target.value. Line twelve is a paragraph, "Hello," comma, and then in curly braces. And line thirteen is the button. Its onClick calls setName with an empty string. The note beside it says it plainly: Clear changes only the state. Now the user types John, and the greeting follows the box letter by letter. In figure two, the name box holds John and the line under it reads, "Hello, John." Then the user clicks Clear. Figure three is the page right after that click, and it looks just like the page when it opened. The box is empty, and the greeting is back to hello with nothing after it. Look at the Clear button once more. Its code only puts an empty string into name. No line of our code touches the box. So who empties the box? The two props on the box do. React understands both of them on every input. onChange is our function, and React calls it every time the user changes the text in the box. Here, it saves the new text in name. And value tells React what the box must show. Here it says, "Show whatever name holds right now." Now the click makes sense. This is what happens in order. The user clicks Clear and setName saves an empty string in name. React renders App again. The greeting reads name, so it shows only hello and the box also reads name through value, so React makes the box empty too. Think of a classroom whiteboard. The students call out their answers, but only the teacher writes on the board. The board shows only what the teacher wrote. Our box works the same way. The user calls out letters through onChange. Only our state writes the text, and the box shows only what state holds through value. A box that works like this is called a controlled box because React state controls what it shows. Principles one and two look at each of the two props on its own.
